stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Derive the net force on the block and its resulting acceleration, and evaluate their numeric values.

(b) Explain how Newton's second law and the assumption of constant kinetic friction justify the computed net force and acceleration.

elements.label: Subtract the opposing friction force, identify the net-force direction, and use Newton's second law to calculate acceleration.
Correctly cites Newton's second law (Fnet = ma) as the governing principle and states that the 6.00 N kinetic friction force is assumed constant while the block slides.

stimulus: A 3.00 kg block is pulled horizontally by 15.0 N while kinetic friction is 6.00 N.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Represent force versus position and determine the work done from x=0 to x=6.0 m.

(b) Determine the cart's speed at x=6.0 m.

(c) The measured travel time is 2.63 s. Determine the average power delivered and explain why the final instantaneous power is different.

elements.label: Represent the applied force as a function of position.
Calculate the work from the area under the force-position graph.
Apply the work-energy theorem.
Calculate the final speed.
Calculate average power.
Calculate and interpret final instantaneous power.

stimulus: A 2.0 kg cart starts from rest on a horizontal frictionless track. The applied force increases uniformly from 2.0 N at x=0 to 14 N at x=6.0 m.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Derive the heat added to the gas during this constant-volume process, and evaluate its numeric value.

(b) Explain how the first law of thermodynamics and the ideal-gas assumption justify treating all the added heat as a change in internal energy at constant volume.

elements.label: W=0 and ΔU=(3/2)nRΔT≈748 J, so Q≈748 J.
Explain how the first law of thermodynamics and the ideal-gas assumption justify treating all the added heat as a change in internal energy at constant volume.

stimulus: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 360 K.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Design a procedure to test how peak induced emf depends on magnet speed.

(b) Identify variables, controls, and a graph.

(c) Predict the voltage trace when the magnet enters and leaves the coil and explain why the entering and leaving pulses have opposite signs.

elements.label: Moves the same magnet through the same coil at several measured speeds and records peak emf.
Keeps magnet orientation/path, coil turns/area, and closest approach fixed.
Plots peak |emf| versus speed and expects an approximately linear trend over a controlled range.
Uses magnet speed as independent variable and peak emf magnitude as dependent variable.
Explains each sign using induced current opposing the corresponding flux change.
Predicts opposite-sign voltage pulses for entering and leaving.

stimulus: A bar magnet moves along the axis of a coil connected to a voltage sensor. The magnet's speed can be controlled.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Derive the energy stored in the capacitor as it is charged from 0 to Q, and evaluate the result in terms of the given quantities.

(b) Explain how the work-energy relation dU=(q/C)dq (the governing principle) and the assumption that C=εA/d stays constant during charging (the stated assumption) support the derived energy.

elements.label: C=εA/d and U=∫₀^Q(q/C)dq=Q²/(2C).
Explain how the work-energy relation dU=(q/C)dq (the governing principle) and the assumption that C=εA/d stays constant during charging (the stated assumption) support the derived energy.

stimulus: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area A, separation d, and dielectric ε; it is charged from 0 to Q.
subject_label: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe a numerical procedure to test Gauss's law for several surfaces.

(b) State controls, a convergence check, and the expected result for surfaces enclosing no charge.

elements.label: Compare each calculated net flux with enclosed charge divided by epsilon0.
Approximates flux by summing E·n ΔA over small surface elements.
Predicts net flux approximately zero for any closed surface enclosing zero net charge, even if local E is nonzero.
Refines surface elements until the flux estimate stabilizes while keeping enclosed charge fixed.

stimulus: A computer model reports electric-field vectors on a fine grid around a localized charged object. Closed surfaces of adjustable size and shape can be drawn.
subject_label: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Derive the mass's velocity v(t) and position x(t) under linear drag, and evaluate the result in terms of the given quantities.

(b) Explain how Newton's second law m dv/dt=-bv, together with the assumption that drag is directly proportional to speed (linear drag) with no other forces acting, leads to the exponential solution for v(t).

elements.label: Solving m dv/dt=-bv gives v(t)=v₀e^{-bt/m} and x(t)=mv₀(1-e^{-bt/m})/b.

Explain how Newton's second law m dv/dt=-bv, together with the assumption that drag is directly proportional to speed (linear drag) with no other forces acting, leads to the exponential solution for v(t).

stimulus: A mass m starts at x(0)=0 with speed v0 and moves through a medium with drag force F=-bv.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question. Use F_T for the string tension and P for the orbital period.

(a) Draw a free-body diagram, label the vertical and inward-radial directions, and translate it into vertical and radial equations.

(b) Using the circular-path radius L sin(theta), derive the angular speed omega and orbital period P in terms of L, g, and theta.

elements.label: Writes F_T cos(theta)=mg and F_T sin(theta)=m omega^2(L sin(theta)), with zero vertical acceleration and inward radial acceleration.
Shows only tension along the string and weight downward.
Eliminates F_T to obtain omega=sqrt(g/(L cos(theta))).
Uses P=2pi/omega to obtain P=2pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g).

stimulus: A mass m on a string of length L moves in a horizontal circle with the string at constant angle theta from vertical, where 0<theta<pi/2.
